Hand-spec'd by Claude Code per the annotation-quality fix spec, Phase 0.3. FLAGGED FOR HUMAN REVIEW before this is treated as ground truth. Two items named in the original spec text ("Heidelburgh Tun" and "tapa") do not actually occur in Chapter 42 -- Heidelburgh Tun is from Chapter 77 ("The Great Heidelburgh Tun"), and no tapa-cloth reference exists in this chapter. Both were dropped as likely misremembered by whoever wrote the spec; the other named examples (albatross, White Steed of the Prairies, albino man, White Squall, Whitsuntide) were verified against the live Gutenberg text and are real. Only the White Steed paragraph is hand-spec'd here per the 'one paragraph' scope in Phase 0.3; the other examples live in nearby paragraphs of the same chapter and are noted but not scored. The passage below matches the real

boundary the pipeline actually annotates against (see paragraphsFromChapterHTML) -- an earlier draft of this file spanned two

paragraphs and never matched a real run.
chapterTitle: Moby-Dick, Chapter 42 -- The Whiteness of the Whale
author: Herman Melville
passage: Most famous in our Western annals and Indian traditions is that of the White Steed of the Prairies; a magnificent milk-white charger, large-eyed, small-headed, bluff-chested, and with the dignity of a thousand monarchs in his lofty, overscorning carriage. He was the elected Xerxes of vast herds of wild horses, whose pastures in those days were only fenced by the Rocky Mountains and the Alleghanies. At their flaming head he westward trooped it like that chosen star which every evening leads on the hosts of light. The flashing cascade of his mane, the curving comet of his tail, invested him with housings more resplendent than gold and silver-beaters could have furnished him. A most imperial and archangelical apparition of that unfallen, western world, which to the eyes of the old trappers and hunters revived the glories of those primeval times when Adam walked majestic as a god, bluff-browed and fearless as this mighty steed. Whether marching amid his aides and marshals in the van of countless cohorts that endlessly streamed it over the plains, like an Ohio; or whether with his circumambient subjects browsing all around at the horizon, the White Steed gallopingly reviewed them with warm nostrils reddening through his cool milkiness; in whatever aspect he presented himself, always to the bravest Indians he was the object of trembling reverence and awe. Nor can it be questioned from what stands on legendary record of this noble horse, that it was his spiritual whiteness chiefly, which so clothed him with divineness; and that this divineness had that in it which, though commanding worship, at the same time enforced a certain nameless terror.

expected_annotations.note: Xerxes I of Persia, remembered for commanding history's largest recorded invasion army; casts the White Steed as sovereign of an ungovernable multitude.
Period spelling of the Allegheny Mountains, used with the Rockies to mark the entire unfenced breadth of the continent.

expected_annotations.anchor: Adam walked majestic as a god
expected_annotations.note: Genesis image of the unfallen Adam in Eden, projecting a prelapsarian, godlike dignity onto both the horse and the American wilderness.
The Ohio River supplies the simile: a herd so vast and continuous it streams over the plains the way a great river runs.

expected_annotations.anchor: commanding worship, at the same time enforced a certain nameless terror
expected_annotations.note: Reading: the steed's divinity is built from the same vocabulary of awe (archangelical, worship, terror) the chapter later attaches to the whale's horror -- Melville is priming the argument that reverence and dread share one root before the essay turns to whiteness's darker instances.
